summary:
MISSION: SECOND CHANCE is an educational browser game made by team hashcode. It shows how spacecraft engineering trade‑offs work when you play the game.

You design a flood‑observation satellite. You pick instruments solar arrays, batteries, an orbit and a launch vehicle. You must balance budget, mass, power, storage and communication limits. Then you run a mission watch targets send data and save energy.

The main feature, Second Chance records your actions. Replays them after you change one component. Keeping all conditions the same lets you see why a pricier design does not always give better science.

The prototype gives resource feedback mission reports, comparison tables, browser saving and downloadable backups. Hardware values and orbital schedules are clearly labelled as assumptions. By linking design choices to what happens during the mission the game shows beginners that success depends on coordinating the system.
details:
MISSION: SECOND CHANCE. Team hashcode

WHAT WE BUILT

I built a browser game that shows beginners how to design a spacecraft and run a mission. The game uses a made‑up flood‑watch mission called Monsoon Watch.

Players choose instruments, solar panels, batteries, an orbit and a launch vehicle. The game then calculates the cost, weight, power needs. Whether the launch is possible. Players then run a 60‑minute simulation broken into twelve five‑minute turns.

Each turn lets players decide to observe send data or save power. The game sets cloud cover, eclipses and communication windows that change the results. Battery power is limited and data counts only after it arrives on Earth.

SECOND CHANCE

The main feature saves every move. Lets you replay the mission after swapping exactly one instrument, solar panel or battery. The orbit, launch vehicle and scheduled conditions stay the same.

The comparison displays the science delivered the battery energy left, the cost, any storage overflow and the final outcome. If a recorded action is no longer possible the replay uses a move and tells you about the change.

In one test swapping the battery for a longer‑life battery raised the cost from 65 to 73 credits and added 90 Wh of energy but the science stayed at 2,880 units. This shows that a pricier part can give power without boosting the science of a chosen plan.

EDUCATIONAL PURPOSE

The game shows how mission goals, hardware, launch limits, communications and science are linked. Players learn by making choices seeing the results failing and comparing outcomes.

NASA’s NISAR mission data helps explain how radar sees through clouds. NASA’s small‑craft communication guide explains data return and power limits. These are just learning references. The game does not use satellite pictures or copy real spacecraft specs.

IMPLEMENTATION

I built the game with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. CSS draws the spacecraft picture. JavaScript does the math runs the mission keeps score replays and saves data locally in the browser. Players can. Import JSON files that hold their design and the original mission record.

ChatGPT helped plan write code explain and debug. I put the files together. Checked the calculations finished the mission, compared replays and restored saved designs in the browser.

MODEL LIMITATIONS

The numbers for hardware, prices, launch limits, weather and orbit times are made up for teaching. The prototype does not compute orbits, full life of the craft or light, on the target. It only works for one player, not for multiplayer.

The result is a working prototype that helps people see engineering trade‑offs and encourages experiments.
